items.title: Colombia: Armed Groups Expand Child Recruitment
items.description: Click to expand Image A 17-year-old boy recruited by the 33rd Front of the EMBF, a dissident group of the demobilized FARC, operating in Colombia’s Catatumbo region near the Venezuelan border. © 2026 Federico Ríos Escobar Child recruitment by armed groups has risen sharply in Colombia in recent years; exploiting poverty, social exclusion, and lack of education to lure children with promises of money, power, and prestige, and increasingly using social media to do so.Colombia has established a range of policies and strategies to prevent child recruitment, and protect and rescue children, but some of these are inadequate and their implementation often falls short. The new administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella should adopt a comprehensive security and justice policy to end these grave human rights violations and ensure that agencies charged with protecting children have the resources and capacity to address this scourge. (Washington, DC) – Child recruitment by armed groups has increased in Colombia as the government has failed to respond effectively, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. August 24, 2026 “I Thought I’d Never See My Mom Again” Recruitment and Use of Children by Colombian Armed Groups Download the full report in English Appendix I: Letter from Meta to Human Rights Watch Appendix II: Email from TikTok to Human Rights Watch The 102-page report, “‘I Thought I’d Never See My Mom Again’: Recruitment and Use of Children by Colombian Armed Groups,” examines the dynamics of child recruitment, the factors that place children at risk, and the strategies and tools used by armed groups, including through social media platforms, to recruit them. Researchers also analyzed the government’s response and its shortcomings in preventing child recruitment, protecting and rescuing children, assisting the reintegration of those who have been released, and prosecuting the individuals responsible. “Armed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity, as protection systems are failing, and social media platforms have become a more effective recruiting ground,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “Every child recruited is indicative of a government failure.” At least 1,500 children have been recruited since 2021, according to Ombudsperson Office data Human Rights Watch reviewed. While comprehensive data is lacking, the official figures available also point to a sharp rise in cases since 2023. Dissident armed groups that emerged from the demobilized Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas are behind the vast majority of reported cases and more than half of the cases are concentrated in Cauca, a southwestern state. Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch Indigenous communities account for nearly half of all reported cases despite making up just 4 percent of Colombia’s population. Over 30 percent were children between the ages of 10 and 14, whose recruitment can be considered a war crime under international law. Human Rights Watch conducted 184 interviews with government officials, humanitarian workers, Indigenous and community leaders, members of human rights and children’s rights organizations, and child protection officers; and held in-person and virtual group meetings with children who had been victims of recruitment or at risk. Researchers reviewed over 70 accounts and 40 posts on social media platforms, such as Facebook and TikTok, that glorified armed group membership and encouraged users to join. Researchers also reviewed and analyzed data from multiple sources, including national institutions and local governments. Armed and criminal groups have taken advantage of poverty, social exclusion, domestic violence, and barriers to education, to recruit children with promises of power, money, and prestige. Children are also recruited through intermediaries and civilian recruiters who are paid up to US$1,000 per child. Recruitment has at times taken place in rural schools, including boarding schools. Armed groups have also taken advantage of social media platforms to glorify life in armed group ranks, make job offers that are essentially ruses aimed at recruiting, and engage with children through public chat forums and private messaging services. These platforms have not effectively detected, removed, or prevented such content. In some cases, their algorithms appeared to promote these posts, most likely expanding the armed groups’ reach. Human Rights Watch contacted both Meta (Facebook) and ByteDance (TikTok) about these findings. Both platforms reported that their policies prohibit the dissemination of content that promotes, supports, and proclaims violent organizations, including Colombian armed groups; and that they have mechanisms in place to prevent its presence in platforms and protect children. Both reported having removed the profiles that Human Rights Watch had flagged to them as containing explicit content of the armed groups, including recruiting offers. Click to expand Image Screenshots from videos posted to TikTok in July 2026 showing the use of emojis to signal affiliation and explicitly seek new combatants for armed groups. Armed groups frequently transfer children to other regions to isolate them, break family and community ties, and make their escape more difficult. In some cases, they receive military training. In others, they are used to gather intelligence, serve as messengers, provide medical care, guard hostages, participate in drug trafficking, or serve as bodyguards for commanders. Girls are particularly exposed to sexual violence. Government policies and strategies to prevent child recruitment, protect and rescue children, and ensure the recovery and reintegration of those released have serious shortcomings, Human Rights Watch found. The National Public Policy on Prevention, passed in 2018, is outdated, and lacks a clear action plan and a dedicated budget. The body charged with coordinating the government response, the Intersectoral Commission for the Prevention of the Recruitment and Use of, and Sexual Violence against, Children and Adolescents (CIPRUNNA), lacks enforcement capacity and the resources needed to implement policies at the local level. Other government efforts are too limited in scope and unable to match the expanding scale of the problem. State and municipal governments face budgetary and capacity constraints that leave many children without protection. The government’s recovery and reintegration efforts for released children have failed to adapt to the new realities of the violence landscape in Colombia, and treat children unequally depending on the nature of the armed group that victimizes them. Those recruited by groups considered parties to the armed conflict enter a specialized program and are eligible for reparations. Children used by armed groups deemed to be criminal groups that are not parties to the armed conflict can be prosecuted or referred to a standard program for children who have suffered abuse. In the absence of meaningful state mechanisms, local community organizations, such as the unarmed guards who protect Indigenous communities, have taken a leading role to protect and support children, and rescue them from armed groups, but at grave risk. Some have been killed in retaliation. The justice system has almost entirely failed child victims of recruitment. In the last decade, roughly 1 percent of the criminal complaints into child recruitment have led to a criminal investigation, and only 0.2 percent resulted in a conviction, most of low-level perpetrators. The new administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella should adopt a comprehensive security and justice policy to end these grave human rights violations, Human Rights Watch said. The government should make sure that the agencies in charge of addressing child recruitment, especially at a municipal level, have enough resources and staff. Crucially, the government should also support, and work with, Indigenous organizations and other local leaders to protect children across Colombia. Social media platforms should conduct human rights due diligence to identify, assess, prevent, mitigate, and account for risks from their systems that may contribute to the recruitment and use of children by armed groups. “Stopping child recruitment will demand much more than just soldiers on the ground,” Goebertus said. “Children at risk of being recruited urgently need opportunities to study and make a living.”

items.title: Pakistan to host South Asian Games in April next year
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan will host the South Asian Games from April 3 to 11 next year, 23 years after it last staged the regional sports gala in Islamabad in 2004. The decision was taken at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the South Asia Olympic Council held here on Sunday, with Pakistan Olympic Association (POA) president Arif Saeed, who is also president of the South Asian Olympic Committee, in the chair. The meeting reviewed preparations for the Games and approved three host cities — Islamabad, Lahore and Peshawar. Representatives from Bangladesh, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka attended the meeting in person, while India participated through video link. All the representatives endorsed the proposed dates, according to sources. A visiting delegation is scheduled to inspect proposed sporting venues in Islamabad on Monday. The Games will feature 28 sports and 346 medal events, with more than 3,200 athletes expected to participate across the three host cities. A large number of technical officials will also be part of the event, with Pakistan preparing to host around 4,000 athletes and other foreign visitors. During Sunday’s meeting, representatives of the participating countries reviewed preparations and measures being taken by Pakistan to host the regional event. The federal government has already given the go-ahead to the POA and other stakeholders to hold the Games and announced that the required funds would be released. Pakistan was originally scheduled to host the Games in 2021, but the event was subsequently postponed for various reasons. Preparations are now said to be in their final stages. The visiting delegation also visited the Taxila Museum and other historical sites on Sunday. Sources said the Capital Development Authority (CDA), on the direction of the federal government, had started preparations to provide accommodation and other facilities to foreign visitors arriving in Islamabad next year for the South Asian Games and other international events, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) conference. “The federal government has been taking every possible step to make the three international events next year in Islamabad highly successful — the South Asian Games, SCO conference and a meeting of the OIC,” a senior government official told Dawn . He said the POA, Foreign Office and federal government were monitoring preparations to ensure that the Games were hosted successfully. “Everyone is on board and working as a team for these Games,” he said. Asked about India’s participation, the official said its representative had joined Sunday’s meeting through video link and endorsed the dates, which, according to him, indicated that India intended to participate. However, another source cautioned that India’s participation could not yet be confirmed. “India has been mixing politics with sports and has avoided visiting Pakistan. Even recently, it did not participate in a volleyball event,” the source said. Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

items.title: Parliament resumes today for five-day sitting amid pending ministerial nominations
items.description: Parliament is set to resume sitting today, Monday, August 24, following a recall by Speaker Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin to enable the House to consider urgent parliamentary business. The five-day sitting will run until Friday, August 28, at Parliament House in Accra, with proceedings scheduled to begin at noon today. The recall was issued by the Speaker on Wednesday, August 12, under Order 58(4) of the Standing Orders of Parliament. Although the Speaker did not specify the matters to be considered during the special sitting, the recall comes at a time when several ministerial nominations from President John Dramani Mahama are awaiting parliamentary consideration. President Mahama has nominated Klottey Korle MP Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings as Minister for Environment, Science and Technology, following the death of the substantive minister, Murtala Mohammed. The President has also nominated Bawku Central MP Mahama Ayariga as Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, alongside the reassignment of two other ministers to new portfolios. The nominations were submitted to Parliament on Friday, August 7, in accordance with Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution, which requires parliamentary approval before ministerial nominees can assume office. Parliament is therefore expected to consider the nominations as part of its business during the five-day recall, including the vetting and approval or rejection of the nominees.

items.title: 50 pick forms to contest 11 NPP executive positions; five eye chairmanship
items.description: Fifty aspirants have picked nomination forms to contest 11 national executive positions in the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) upcoming national executive elections, with five of them seeking the National Chairperson position. The five are Paul Afoko, John Boadu, Boakye Agyarko, Sammy Crabbe, and Bernard Antwi Boasiako. The incumbent National Chairman, Mr Stephen Ayesu Ntim, is not seeking re-election. For the General Secretary position, incumbent Justin Kodua Frimpong is seeking a second term and faces competition from Eugene Boakye Antwi, Sylvester Tetteh and Charles Dwamena. Eight aspirants picked forms for the National Organiser position. They are Glover Daniel Nii Kwartei, Salam Mustapha, Kwame Prempeh, Archibald Korletey Gamor, Emmanuel Korsi Bodja, Nana Kwadjo Agyei Yeboah, Daniel Agyenim Boateng and Ali Maiga Halidu. The National Youth Organiser position has attracted six aspirants: Clement Opoku Gyamfi, Chris Lloyd Nii Kwei Asamoah, Michael Osei Boateng, Vera Oye Bram-Larbi, Kumi Alfred Ababio and Abanga Fuseini Yakubu. Three aspirants picked forms to contest the National Women Organiser position. They are Mavis Hawa Koomson, Perpetual Ekua Lomokie Akwada, and Safia Mohammed. The National Communications Director position has two aspirants – Dennis Miracles Aboagye and Evans Kodo. Gordon Asare Bediako, who had expressed interest in the Communications Director position, withdrew from the race on Saturday and endorsed Mr Aboagye. For the National Vice Chairperson position, 13 aspirants picked forms. They include Henry Nana Boakye, Kojo Fosu Boadu, Mustapha Abdul Hameed, Samuel Pyne, Richard Ahiagba, Abena Pokua Boaitey Amoah, Alhaji Masawudu Osman, Yaa Amponsah Frimpong, George Kwabena Abankwah Yeboah, Horma Miez, Richard Oti Aboagye, Bright Esselfie Kumi and Nana Akomea. The National Treasurer position attracted four aspirants – Alfred Kojo Thompson, Collins Nuntwiri Nuamah, Tahiru Issahaku Moomin and Ahmed Ruka Saida. Five aspirants picked forms for the National Nasara Organiser position. They are Issaka Muazo Kunata, Salim Bamba, Razak Tahiru Maiga, Awal Mohammed and Mohammed Ali Suraj. The NPP National Officers Elections Committee said the purchase or collection of a nomination form did not, by itself, constitute a valid nomination or candidature. An aspirant would become a nominee only after properly filing the completed nomination form and accompanying documents within the prescribed period, subject to vetting and other processes required under the party’s constitution and election regulations, it said. Filing of completed nomination forms commenced on Sunday, August 23, and will close on Saturday, August 29, 2026. The nominees will subsequently be vetted from Monday, August 31, to Thursday, September 3, 2026. The committee said the date for balloting had not yet been fixed because it wanted the filing, vetting and possible appeals processes to be completed before determining the final field of candidates.

items.title: Getting heard in Parliament currently is difficult – Afenyo-Markin
items.description: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin says that getting the Minority’s voice heard in Parliament has become difficult due to the Majority’s numerical strength. Speaking on Joy News’ The Probe on Sunday, he said the Minority has to work harder to ensure its views are heard despite having fewer MPs. “It is a very difficult one because you are in opposition, and you need to work hard with your colleagues to ensure that, notwithstanding your numbers, your voice is heard,” he said. The Effutu MP said the current parliamentary arithmetic presents a major challenge for the Minority, with the Majority holding 189 seats. “So, getting your voice heard in a chamber where the majority is 189 can be very difficult,” he said. He also pointed to the leadership of Parliament as another factor that makes the Minority’s task challenging. “You have a speaker who is not on your side in terms of party affiliation, and you have a first deputy who is also part of the majority, and obviously, his first mandate will be to protect his side,” he said. According to him, the situation requires the Minority to adopt a deliberate approach to its work in Parliament. “So it calls for a lot of hard work, determination, and a focused strategy to make sure that you navigate well,” he said. Afenyo-Markin, however, said the Minority is not intimidated by its current numbers. He said the New Patriotic Party has previously operated in Parliament with a much smaller representation and still managed to grow its numbers. “This is not the first time NPP is getting into the chamber with fewer numbers,” he said. He cited the Second Parliament, when the NPP had 61 MPs against the National Democratic Congress’s 133. “You may recall that in 1992 we didn’t participate in the parliamentary elections. So, in the second parliament, we had 61, led by J. H. Mensah, and the NDC had 133,” he said. Afenyo-Markin said the NPP later increased its parliamentary representation to 102 by the 2000 election. “But through their industry, by the 2000 election, that 61 increased to 102,” he said. He insisted that the current 87-member Minority would not be discouraged by the numbers. “So I’m not perturbed at all by the numbers today. We’re 87. We say we are a mighty minority,” he said. items.title: GHS launches strategic PHEOC documents to strengthen public health emergency response
items.description: The Ghana Health Service (GHS) has launched five strategic documents to help strengthen public health emergency preparedness and response across the country. The event saw the launch of the strategic National Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC) documents and the presentation of a national roadmap for the operationalisation of PHEOC across Ghana. The five documents launched were the National PHEOC Strategic Plan 2026-2030, National PHEOC Handbook 2026, and National PHEOC Standard Operating Procedures, Volume One. The others are the National Health Workforce Search and Strategy Plan 2026-2034 and the National Public Health Workforce Search and Management SOP, Volume Two. The documents were developed through collaboration among the Ministry of Health, GHS, security and emergency services, academia, research institutions, professional bodies, civil society and private-sector stakeholders. This formed part of efforts by the service to build a more resilient, coordinated and sustainable public health emergency management system. Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, the Director-General of the GHS, said the launch marked an important step in strengthening Ghana’s national health security. He said public health emergencies required a unified response from all relevant institutions, adding: “When disease spreads, success is not determined by plans left on the shelf. It is determined by our capacity to act as one unified system.” Dr Akoriyea said early detection, timely treatment and prompt care were critical to saving lives as Ghana had experienced seasonal outbreaks of meningitis, cholera, typhoid and other diseases. The Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, he said, would help bridge the gap between data collection and strategic action. “PHEOC would also connect health agencies, emergency services, laboratories and animal health agencies” he noted, adding that the centre would help provide a platform for coordinated action during public health emergencies. It would also support the implementation of the International Health Regulations and address gaps identified through joint external evaluations. He noted that Ghana had learnt important lessons from major disease outbreaks, including the COVID-19 pandemic, saying the focus must now shift from documents to action and from preparedness on paper to readiness in practice. He called for a functional, connected and sustainable emergency response system. Dr Lawrence Lartey, Head of the National PHEOC, said the implementation strategy focused on seven key areas. These include governance and institutionalisation, ICT and public health intelligence, logistics and infrastructure, emergency operations and incident management, workforce capacity, sustainability and multispectral coordination. Dr Lartey said the strategy would promote the use of integrated dashboards and other digital systems to support timely decision making. He said logistics and infrastructure would also be strengthened to support rapid deployment during outbreaks and emergencies, adding that trained and skilled workforce was necessary for effective emergency response. Dr Lartey said the strategy would connect emergency operations at the national, regional, district and community levels, aimed to establish one coordinated system with common standards and shared situational awareness. He said regular testing, monitoring and after-action reviews would help improve the health system while sustainable financing and accountability would also be critical to the success of the PHEOC. Domestic financing must be strengthened while partner support was properly aligned, Dr Lartey said, and that “The launch is not the destination. It is a transition to implementation.”

items.title: Oti NPP Communication Director alleges region receives fewer birds under ‘Nkoko nkitinkiti’; NDC debunks claim
items.description: Seidu Musah, Oti Regional Communication Director of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), has alleged that only 810 birds under the government’s ‘Nkoko Nkitinkiti’ initiative have been brought to the Oti Region, claiming that the beneficiaries were largely members of the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC). He questioned whether the reported number of birds was sufficient to meet the needs of beneficiaries across the region, considering the population, number of communities and the size of the NDC’s membership in the Oti Region. Mr Musah made the allegation in an exclusive interview with the Ghana News Agency (GNA) to assess the performance of the NDC government in the region since assuming office. He said the government had been in office for about one-and-a-half years and was approaching its second year, but, in his assessment, there were no significant tangible achievements to show its tenure in the region. According to him, the government had made several promises to the people of Oti, but the pace of implementation of those commitments had fallen short of residents’ expectations. He also called for greater transparency in the implementation of the Nkoko Nkitinkiti initiative, particularly regarding the number of birds supplied to the region, the criteria for selecting beneficiaries, and their geographical distribution. He said such information would enable the public to assess whether the programme was being implemented fairly and achieving its intended objective of supporting livelihoods. Mr Musah said the NPP would continue to monitor government programmes and policies in the region and hold the government accountable for its promises. He, however, acknowledged that government programmes should ultimately be assessed based on their impact on ordinary citizens rather than political considerations. Mr Musah urged the government to prioritise projects and interventions that would directly improve the livelihoods of farmers, young people, women and small-scale entrepreneurs. Ghana News Agency investigations reveal otherwise as confirmed by Mr Williams Ntoso, Oti Deputy Director of Communication of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), who refuted Mr Musah’s claim, describing the allegation as untrue. He said the Nkoko Nkitinkiti initiative had not supplied only 810 birds to the region as alleged. According to Mr Ntoso, each of the nine Municipal and District Assemblies in the Oti Region received 10,000 birds under the programme, bringing the total number supplied to the region to 90,000 birds. He therefore urged the public to disregard the claim that only 810 birds had been brought to the region, saying the actual figure was 90,000. The NDC Deputy Regional Communication Director maintained that the programme was being implemented across the region and was intended to support beneficiaries and improve livelihoods.

items.title: La dérive des comptes publics américains se poursuit
items.description: Fin juillet, la dette publique de l’État fédéral a dépassé pour la première fois le seuil des 40 000 milliards de dollars, soit 123 % du PIB. Elle se rapproche désormais du dernier plafond approuvé par le Congrès, fixé à 41 100 milliards de dollars. Ce dernier devrait être atteint avant la fin de l’année, ce qui donnera lieu à l'un de ces événements récurrents visant à le rehausser afin d’éviter un nouveau shutdown du gouvernement fédéral. Contrairement à ce qu’il avait promis, Donald Trump n’a pas réduit le déficit de l’État. À 1 800 milliards de dollars fin juillet pour l’année fiscale 2026 (qui a commencé en octobre 2025), le déficit américain n’a été supérieur que lors de l'année 2021, en raison de la pandémie de Covid-19. Le Congressional Budget Office prévoit un déficit de 2 100 milliards de dollars pour l’ensemble de l’année fiscale, soit 6,5 % du PIB. Les intérêts payés par l’État fédéral sur sa dette ont augmenté de 14 % entre l’année fiscale 2025 et 2026, en raison notamment de la hausse des taux d’intérêt. Les dépenses de Sécurité sociale, de Medicaid et de Medicare ont augmenté de 7 % sous l’effet du vieillissement de la population, tandis que celles consacrées aux nombreux vétérans de l’armée américaine ont augmenté de 11 %. Les dépenses de Défense ont quant à elles augmenté de 5 %. Les dépenses du département fédéral de l’éducation ont diminué de 79 milliards de dollars, soit -60 %, celles de l'Environmental Protection Agency de 20 milliards, soit -59 %, et les aides internationales de 10 milliards, soit -36 %. Côté recettes, les rentrées d'impôts sur le revenu des ménages ont augmenté de 161 milliards de dollars, soit 7 %, malgré les baisses d'impôts pour les foyers les plus aisés. Les droits de douane ont quant à eux augmenté de 18 milliards de dollars, soit une hausse de 13 %, et ce, en dépit de l'annulation par la Cour suprême de la plupart des droits de douane imposés par Donald Trump. En revanche, les impôts sur les bénéfices des entreprises ont reculé de 89 milliards, soit une baisse de 23 %. Cette dérive des comptes publics, combinée aux effets de la guerre en Iran et à la politique économique erratique de Donald Trump, a entraîné une forte hausse des taux d’intérêt sur la dette publique américaine : les taux sur les bons du Trésor américain à 30 ans ont dépassé pour la première fois les 5 % depuis 2007, avant la crise financière de 2008. Si les taux d’intérêt auxquels l’État américain doit s’endetter se stabilisaient durablement à 5 %, l’État fédéral devrait payer chaque année, avec sa dette actuelle, 2 000 milliards d’intérêts, soit 6,3 % du PIB, soit deux fois le budget annuel de la défense. Un tel niveau de taux entraînerait de façon quasi certaine un effet boule de neige et une crise de la dette américaine. Cette dégradation rapide des conditions de financement de l’État fédéral américain traduit le fait que, sur les marchés financiers, il y a désormais plus d'acteurs qui cherchent à vendre des bons du Trésor qu'à en acheter. Alors qu'ils étaient jusqu'alors considérés comme l'actif sûr par excellence par tous les investisseurs à l'échelle mondiale, les bons du Trésor américain sont désormais menacés de ne plus l'être. Si ce sentiment devait persister, la défiance pourrait s’aggraver et les taux d’intérêt sur la dette américaine pourraient atteindre des niveaux encore plus élevés. C'est pour casser cette dynamique que Scott Bessent, le secrétaire au Trésor américain, a décidé de doubler, à partir du 9 septembre, le programme de rachat des titres de dette américains à long terme qu’il avait déjà initié. Pour l’instant, cette annonce n’a entraîné aucun reflux des taux d’intérêt sur la dette américaine à long terme. Une telle politique relève de l’expédient et ne change rien au déficit américain, ni donc au volume global de dette supplémentaire à contracter. Cela consiste simplement à accroître la part de la dette à court terme, pour laquelle les taux d’intérêt sont inférieurs, au sein de la dette fédérale globale. Mais un État qui dépend d’une dette à court terme est en réalité plus fragile et plus dépendant des fluctuations des marchés financiers, car il doit emprunter davantage chaque année pour couvrir son déficit et rembourser le capital des dettes à court terme qu’il a contractées. En réalité, la Réserve fédérale américaine est le seul acteur qui puisse réellement limiter les taux d’intérêt à long terme sur la dette américaine. Confrontée à la crise provoquée par la pandémie de Covid-19, elle a fortement baissé les taux d’intérêt à long terme en rachetant des montants colossaux de titres de dette publique, pour un total de plus de 3 000 milliards de dollars entre 2020 et 2022. Elle avait ensuite cessé ses achats et réduit progressivement son encours. Depuis décembre dernier, elle a recommencé à acheter de la dette publique américaine, à hauteur, pour le moment, de 350 milliards de dollars. Il en faudrait cependant beaucoup plus pour faire baisser les taux longs américains. Mais si la Fed se remettait vraiment à faire du quantitative easing à grande échelle, cela risquerait d’avoir un effet inflationniste important, alors que la hausse des prix du pétrole, due à la guerre contre l’Iran, et les tarifs douaniers de Donald Trump poussent déjà les prix à la hausse aux États-Unis. L’article La dérive des comptes publics américains se poursuit est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Our voice must be heard – Afenyo-Markin warns Majority against taking NPP’s 87 MPs for granted
items.description: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has warned the governing majority against taking the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) 87 MPs for granted, insisting that the Minority’s voice must be heard in Parliament. Speaking on Joy News’ The Probe on Sunday, the Effutu MP acknowledged the difficulty of leading a smaller caucus in a chamber where the governing side has 189 MPs. He said the Minority must work harder to ensure its concerns receive attention despite its numerical disadvantage. “Well, it’s a very difficult one because you are in opposition, and you need to work hard with your colleagues to ensure that, notwithstanding your numbers, your voice is heard.” Mr Afenyo-Markin said the task is made more challenging by the composition of Parliament’s leadership. “You have a speaker who is not on your side in terms of party affiliation, and you have a first deputy who is also part of the majority, and obviously, his first mandate will be to protect his side.” He said the situation requires the NPP caucus to adopt a deliberate approach to parliamentary business. “So it calls for a lot of hard work, determination, and a focused strategy to make sure that you navigate well.” Despite the current numbers, Mr Afenyo-Markin said he is not intimidated by the size of the governing majority. He pointed to the NPP’s history in Parliament to argue that a smaller caucus can grow through sustained work. “This is not the first time NPP is getting into the chamber with fewer numbers.” He recalled that the NPP had 61 MPs in the Second Parliament after it did not participate in the 1992 parliamentary elections. “You may recall that in 1992 we didn’t participate in the parliamentary elections. So, in the second parliament, we had 61, led by J. H. Mensah, and the NDC had 133.” According to him, the party’s parliamentary fortunes improved significantly in the years that followed. “But through their industry, by the 2000 election, that 61 increased to 102.” He said that history gives him confidence that the current 87-member caucus can also make an impact. “So I’m not perturbed at all by the numbers today. We’re 87. We say we are a mighty minority. We feel the might in the substance we put out, and we are not intimidated by the numbers.” Mr Afenyo-Markin stressed that the Minority’s effectiveness should not be measured solely by its numerical strength. “Our voice must be heard, and when people hear us, they must see substance in us.” He said the focus, therefore, remains on ensuring the NPP caucus is heard and its contributions carry weight in Parliament.

items.title: NPP Oti Executives set sights on 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections
items.description: The newly elected Regional Executives of the New Patriotic Party (NPP) in the Oti Region have pledged to work towards securing victory for the party’s flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, in the 2028 presidential election. The executives have also resolved to strengthen the party’s structures across the region and develop effective strategies to win parliamentary seats in the 2028 general election after the party failed to secure any parliamentary seat in the region in the 2024 elections. Speaking to the Ghana News Agency (GNA) after an engagement of the newly constituted Regional Executive Committee, Dr Frank Yirenkyi, Regional Chairman, said the new administration was committed to rebuilding and strengthening the party from the grassroots to the constituency level. He said the leadership would engage party members across all constituencies, identify challenges affecting the party, and work collectively to address them in preparation for the 2028 elections. “Our mandate is to work very hard in all the constituencies to make sure that we win the parliamentary seat elections,” he said. Dr Yirenkyi, however, declined to disclose the number of parliamentary seats the party was targeting, explaining that the new administration had only recently assumed office and would first undertake consultations before developing a comprehensive electoral strategy. “Presently, I can’t tell you because we just took office. We are going to work, we are going to strategise and then come out with a solution on how to accomplish it,” he said. He said the party’s immediate priority was to strengthen its internal structures, improve coordination among the various constituencies, and mobilise members and supporters towards a common objective. Concerning possible divisions following the regional elections, Dr Yirenkyi said the elections were conducted peacefully and fairly, with no major grievances brought to the attention of the new leadership. He said he had engaged other stakeholders within the party to promote unity, reconciliation and cooperation among members, stressing that unity would be critical to the party’s prospects in the 2028 elections. According to him, the peaceful atmosphere that characterised the declaration of the election results and subsequent engagements was an indication of the willingness of members to work together despite differences that might have emerged during the electoral process. He said the newly elected executives had also held their maiden meeting, during which members interacted cordially and demonstrated their commitment to working together in the interest of the party. The Chairman reaffirmed his commitment to promoting unity and inclusiveness within the party, saying the NPP could only achieve its political objectives through collective effort and effective collaboration. “My mandate is to unite the party. We are going to work together to deliver to our people,” he added. Dr Yirenkyi appealed to party members, supporters and sympathisers to remain united, disciplined and committed as the party intensified preparations towards the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections. He said the Regional Executive Committee would continue to engage stakeholders and grassroots members to build a stronger, more cohesive and competitive party capable of reclaiming parliamentary representation in the region and contributing to the election of Dr Bawumia as President in 2028.

items.title: CDF Munir to visit Tehran on Monday, says Iranian foreign ministry
items.description: Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir will visit Tehran on Monday to continue efforts to bring peace ​and security to the region, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil ‌Baqaei said on Sunday, according to a statement by the ministry. He said CDF Munir would lead an official delegation and the “visit aims to strengthen bilateral cooperation between Iran and Pakistan and to continue Pakistan’s good offices in support of peace and security in the region”. During the visit, CDF Munir would meet and hold talks with senior officials Iran, Baqaei added. The visit comes amid heightened tensions as ‌Iran threatens ⁠a military response to US plans for sanctions that could further put a strain on the Islamic republic’s ailing economy. It will coincide with a Monday announcement on details related to the planned sanctions, which ​US officials have ​said would be “ the ⁠toughest sanctions in history ” on Iran. Trump had warned of economic consequences against any country that provided “any type ​of lifeline to Iran” as he seeks to isolate ​the ⁠Islamic republic. Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorised oil tankers that ⁠try to ​transit the vital waterway, and Iran’s ​economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions. Pakistan’s mediation Pakistan has been leading mediation efforts between the two sides in the ongoing war, which began with US and ​Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Less than two months after the beginning of the war, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between the two sides on April 8 and Islamabad hosted direct talks between US and Iran on April 11 and 12. The mediation efforts also led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on June 17 between the US and Iran in Geneva. The MoU set a framework to move towards a permanent end to the war. While hostilities have renewed between the two sides since, Pakistan remains engaged in mediation efforts, with CDF Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi having made multiple visits to Iran in recent months.

items.title: NAPO calls for evidence-based reassessment of Busia’s administration in the Second Republic
items.description: Dr Matthew Opoku Prempeh, the 2024 Vice Presidential candidate of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), has called for an evidence-based reassessment of the administration of Professor Kofi Abrefa Busia. He noted that Ghana’s Second Republic should neither be romanticised nor judged solely by the military coup that ended it. The administration should be assessed on its constitutional philosophy, policy choices, development record, shortcomings and the historical conditions under which it governed, he said. “Belonging to a tradition does not oblige me to flatter it,” Dr Prempeh said, arguing that historical judgement required evidence, context and proportion. He made the call in a keynote address at the 2026 Busia Institute Lecture held at the London Hilton on Park Lane, United Kingdom (UK), on Sunday, August 9, 2026. The lecture, organised by the Busia Institute for Rural and Democratic Development, in collaboration with the Young Executive Forum, UK, was on the theme: “Centre-Right Political Thought in Africa: The Ghanaian Experience.” It was to examine the historical development and contemporary relevance of centre-right political thought in Ghana with intellectual independence. Prof Busia served as the Prime Minister of Ghana in the Second Republic from 1969 until his government was overthrown in 1972. Dr Prempeh said the Second Republic restored elected civilian government, Parliament, fundamental rights and judicial authority after a period of military rule, which sought to translate its political philosophy into programmes in rural development, education, Ghanaian participation in the economy, decentralisation and private enterprise. He said the military overthrow of the Progress Party Government in January 1972 could not constitute a legitimate democratic verdict on the administration because it prevented citizens from assessing the government through elections. He, nevertheless, acknowledged that some decisions of the administration remained controversial. On the 1969 Aliens Compliance Order, Dr Prempeh described the human consequences suffered by affected migrants as a “wound”, and said the legitimate power of a state to regulate immigration had to be distinguished from the manner in which a policy was implemented. “The legitimate purpose of the policy is one thing. The manner of its execution is another,” he said. Dr Prempeh argued that political traditions could not survive on historical reputation alone, adding that, “A political party earns its place not by winning offices, but by becoming an institution of memory, of ideas and of honest leadership.” He urged present-day adherents of the Danquah-Dombo-Busia tradition to address contemporary problems, including youth opportunity, technology, modern agriculture, inequality and the performance of public institutions. He called on the Ghanaian diaspora to contribute knowledge, professional expertise, investment networks and institutional experience alongside remittances. Former President John Agyekum Kufuor, Life Patron of the Busia Institute, said Ghana’s centre-right tradition had historically rested on constitutional government, liberty under law, a free press, private enterprise, social responsibility, decentralisation and opposition to arbitrary rule. He urged political actors to protect Parliament, the Judiciary, the media and independent constitutional institutions to safeguard democracy and to regard public office as a temporary trust. “An opponent remains a fellow citizen, and a temporary majority does not own the republic,” Mr Kufuor said. He pointed out that Prof Busia’s record had often been assessed without sufficient regard to the fact that his government was in office for only 27 months. He cited rural development, agriculture, health facilities, support for smallholder farmers, technical and vocational training and decentralisation among programmes pursued by the administration. Mr Bernard Owusu, Chairman of the lecture and a senior Ghanaian-British legal practitioner, said strong institutions were indispensable to democratic life. “Democracy is not simply about elections,” he said. “It is about values, habits, discipline, citizenship, tolerance and respect for the rule of law.” Dr Anane Agyei, the Executive Director of the Busia Institute, said political traditions should be assessed according to the ideas they defended, the institutions they built, the manner in which they exercised public authority and their consequences for citizens. The London event was the first Busia Institute Lecture held outside Ghana and was attended by diplomats, Members of Parliament, Ghanaian professionals, and members of the Ghanaian diaspora among other guests.

items.title: Nigeria’s oil output wobbles after 10yrs of increase in rigs
items.description: Output drops 20.8% in five mature assets — Report Nigeria’s influence within OPEC+ declines We are committed to optimising output — Renaissance, Eni Bad omen requiring urgent steps — Experts By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor There are indications that increased deployment of oil rigs in Nigeria has not translated into corresponding rise in crude oil production. Rig count, an important indicator of exploration and production activities, is generally expected to support higher crude oil output as operators drill new wells, maintain existing assets and develop additional reserves. But official records show that oil output has stagnated over the period since 2016 when rig count was at its peak in Nigeria’s oil fields. Industry experts told Financial Vanguard that the situation is attributable to a declining output from oil wells described as mature fields as well as slow development of new wells. According to data obtained from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, OPEC, a total of 2,099 rigs were deployed in Nigeria between 2016 and 2026, representing investments running into billions of US dollars. The data showed that 360 rigs were utilised in 2018, the highest annual deployment during the period, while 87 rigs were recorded in 2021, the lowest. Checks by Financial Vanguard indicated that deepwater drilling can cost between US$400,000 and US$600,000 per day for the rig alone, excluding drilling mud, casing, cementing, logistics, helicopters, supply vessels, insurance and other services. A single offshore exploration well can cost between US$50 million and more than US$150 million, depending on water depth and complexity, meaning that Nigeria’s exploration campaigns have involved investments running into billions of dollars. Despite the spending, Nigeria recorded its highest crude oil output (excluding condensate) amounting to 1.734 million barrels per day, bpd, in 2019, a figure that is significantly below annual budget projection. It even declined to 1.143 million bpd in 2022. Output drops 20.8% in five mature assets — Report Meanwhile, Nigeria’s average oil output from five mature producing fields fell 20.8 per cent year-on-year, YoY, to 10,930 bpd in June 2026 from 13,794 bpd in June 2025, highlighting the pressure on national production and revenue. A mature oil asset is a field that has produced for many years and moved beyond its early development and peak production stages. Such fields typically experience declining reservoir pressure, increasing water production and falling output, requiring additional investment and enhanced recovery measures to sustain production. Data obtained from the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, NUPRC, showed that Abo oil field, operated by Eni/Agip and producing since 2003, recorded a 39.2 per cent YoY decline to 6,870 bpd in June 2026 from 11,297 bpd in June 2025. Pennington, operated by Pennington Producing Limited, fell 45 per cent to 3,880 bpd from 7,107 bpd, while Ugo Ocha, also known as Jones Creek, declined 16.6 per cent to 26,900 bpd from 32,246 bpd. Sea Eagle, operated by Renaissance Energy, dropped 8.3 per cent to 14,570 bpd from 15,886 bpd, while Okwori, operated by Antan Producing Limited, declined marginally to 2,430 bpd from 2,435 bpd. Investigations across Abia, Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Edo, Imo, Ondo and Rivers states showed that many fields have experienced significant depletion since Nigeria’s first commercial oil discovery in 1956. While some operators have invested in additional wells, workovers and other measures to sustain production, others have struggled to commit the required capital, contributing to declining and unstable output. We are committed to optimising output — Renaissance, Eni Responding to Financial Vanguard’s enquiries, Renaissance Africa Energy, operator of Sea Eagle, said the field’s decline was consistent with its maturity. “Sea Eagle, a Renaissance JV asset, is a mature field and its production performance remains broadly in line with expectations set out in the approved Field Development Plan. As is typical for mature assets, the field is experiencing a natural production decline associated with field life cycle progression. “The current production profile of Sea Eagle has been factored into Renaissance’s business and growth plans and has not had a material impact on the company’s operations. Sea Eagle represents a relatively small proportion of Renaissance’s overall production portfolio. “Renaissance continues to evaluate and implement opportunities to optimise production and maximise value from its assets in line with approved development plans, regulatory requirements and long-term business objectives. The company remains focused on sustaining operational reliability and pursuing initiatives that support the efficient development of its asset base.” Similarly, Eni stated in an email response to Financial Vanguard: “Nigeria’s deep offshore Abo field produced its first oil in April 2003 and has remained consistently in production for the past 23 years, a remarkable achievement. This longevity is further evidenced by its current production performance, which aligns with the asset’s maturity. To sustain this, output optimisation measures are being implemented, including upgrades to gas compressors.” Nigeria’s influence within OPEC+ declines Checks by Financial Vanguard also showed that Nigeria’s influence within OPEC and the broader global oil market has weakened as production has remained below its historical levels. Nigeria’s crude oil production peaked at about 2.5 million bpd in November 2005, according to historical production data, making the country a major force within OPEC and the international oil market. However, despite post-Petroleum Industry Act, PIA, investment efforts, national output, including condensate, has not gone beyond 1.7 million bpd. Nigeria was also not among the seven OPEC+ countries that held a virtual meeting on August 2, 2026, to review global oil market conditions and the production outlook. According to OPEC: “In their collective commitment to support oil market stability, the seven participating countries decided to implement a production adjustment of 188 thousand barrels per day from the additional voluntary adjustments announced in April 2023. “This adjustment will be implemented in September 2026. “The seven OPEC+ countries also noted that this measure will provide an opportunity for the participating countries to accelerate their compensation. “The seven countries reiterated their collective commitment to achieve full conformity with the Declaration of Cooperation, including the additional voluntary production adjustments that will be monitored by the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC). “They also confirmed their intention to fully compensate for any over-produced volume since January 2024. The seven OPEC+ countries will continue to hold monthly meetings to review market conditions.” The seven OPEC+ countries are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman. The latest OPEC+ production adjustment has underscored Nigeria’s limited capacity to take advantage of higher production opportunities. Industry analysts have warned that the country risks losing significant revenue because ageing fields, underinvestment, crude theft, pipeline vandalism and delays in developing new projects continue to constrain output. While several OPEC+ members are adjusting production to influence global prices and maximise revenues, Nigeria continues to struggle to produce enough crude to meet its OPEC allocation and growing demand from new domestic refineries. Bad omen requiring urgent steps — Experts An industry expert who pleaded anonymity said Nigeria must combine exploration with aggressive field development and enhanced recovery from existing assets. “Exploration must be accompanied by aggressive field development, enhanced recovery from mature assets, improved security, infrastructure upgrades and faster regulatory approvals. “Nigeria already possesses substantial proven reserves, and the greater challenge is converting those reserves into sustained production rather than simply discovering additional hydrocarbons. “Unless these structural constraints are addressed, increased exploration spending alone is unlikely to deliver the higher crude oil output needed to boost government revenue, improve foreign exchange earnings and strengthen Nigeria’s position in the global oil market. “Efforts should also be intensified to complete some planned oil and gas projects, including Bonga North, Southwest/Aparo, Zabazaba, and Etan in order to enhance Nigeria’s oil output.” In a telephone interview with Financial Vanguard, Chairman/Chief Executive Officer of Brittania-U, Catherine Uju Ifejika, stressed the importance of additional investment in mature assets, citing the company’s Ajapa field. She said more than $400 million was invested after Brittania-U acquired the asset from Chevron, including the drilling of additional wells and deployment of a Floating Production, Storage and Offloading, FPSO, facility. According to her, the investment enabled Ajapa to commence production at about 2,300 bpd in 2010, followed by increased and more stable output. Also speaking with Financial Vanguard, Wumi Iledare, Professor Emeritus of Petroleum Economics, said the NUPRC’s findings on mature and declining fields highlighted a structural challenge that affects both production and public revenue. “Declining production translates directly into reduced government revenue, weaker external reserves, lower foreign-exchange inflows, and diminished economic value creation. The policy response should therefore go beyond passive acceptance of natural decline. “Nigeria must actively optimise remaining production through faster regulatory approvals, incentives for re-entering selected abandoned wells, infill drilling, workovers, artificial-lift optimisation, and deployment of proven enhanced oil recovery technologies where commercially viable. “The Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) already recognises the maturity profile of Nigeria’s oil fields. Its production allowances and progressive royalty structure reflect a key petroleum-economic principle: fiscal terms must balance government take with the need to sustain investment in recovering remaining reserves. “A barrel that remains underground due to commercial or regulatory disincentives generates no revenue for government, no return for investors, and no value for the economy. “The core challenge, therefore, is not simply increasing production, but maximising economic recovery from existing assets within their remaining productive life.” He added: “This is the essence of petroleum asset optimisation — and ultimately, public value optimisation.” The post Nigeria’s oil output wobbles after 10yrs of increase in rigs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Upper East: NRSA sensitises commercial motorbike, tricycle riders on new regulations
items.description: The National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) has sensitised commercial motorbike and tricycle operators in the Upper East Region on new regulations governing their operations. The new regulations, Ghana’s Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (Legislative Instrument 2519), passed by Parliament in December 2025 and came into force in 2026, is part of efforts to improve road safety and reduce crashes. The new LI also provides legal backing for the commercial use of motorcycles and tricycles in Ghana. The sensitisation formed part of a six-month transition period to educate operators and other stakeholders on the requirements of Legislative Instrument (LI) 2519. Mr Eric Anokye Fordjour, the Upper East Regional Head of the NRSA, said the new regulations would provide a structured framework for commercial motorcycle and tricycle operations while improving the quality of service provided to passengers. He noted that one of the key requirements was for every commercial operator to belong to a recognised union, which would enable the authorities and the unions to better supervise operators and ensure compliance. Mr Fordjour added the regulations also placed strong emphasis on safety, particularly the mandatory use of crash helmets by commercial motorbike riders, citing the high incidence of motorcycle crashes and fatalities associated with non-use of helmets. He said the Authority would intensify engagement with executives of the operators’ unions to ensure that education translated into compliance. “We believe that with the intensified education, the compliance will follow,” he stated. Mr Fordjour said the ultimate expectation was for the new measures to contribute to a reduction in road crashes and save lives. Mr Prince David Orchill, Senior Finance Officer at the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), announced that persons seeking to operate commercial motorcycles and tricycles must be at least 21 years old. He said although a person could obtain a private driving licence at 18, a commercial licence could only be issued after attaining 21 years. He urged parents and operators not to allow persons below the stipulated age to operate commercial motorcycles or tricycles, warning that doing so constituted a breach of the law. Mr Orchill said applicants for commercial rider licences were also required to present their Ghana Card number and pass the requisite medical examinations, including physical and eye tests. Mr Orchill said commercial vehicles would be required to undergo roadworthiness testing every six months, compared with the one-year interval applicable to private vehicles. He cautioned operators that possessing a valid licence did not exempt them from complying with road safety regulations, explaining that licences could be revoked where an operator was found to have engaged in dangerous driving. Mr Yakubu Ayamga, the Upper East Regional Chairman of the National Union of Tricycle Operators Ghana, welcomed the new regulations and pledged the union’s support for their implementation. He said the lack of regularisation had previously allowed some operators to act without proper control, creating challenges for both authorities and other road users. Mr Ayamga indicated that the new framework would bring the relevant authorities and operators together to streamline tricycle operations and promote discipline on the roads. He pledged to extend the education to members of the union and urged operators to cooperate with passengers.

items.title: How 23 stocks beat inflation
items.description: ***6 coys didn’t declare dividend ***7 coys record negative Return On Equity By Peter Egwatu Twenty-three stocks quoted on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) have delivered returns well above Nigeria’s inflation rate so far in 2026, providing investors with significant nominal gains despite a challenging macroeconomic environment. An analysis of selected companies’ stock performance by Vanguard showed that the strongest performers had posted price appreciation of between about 94 per cent and 365 per cent year-to-date (YtD) as of August 2026, comfortably exceeding the reported average inflation rate of about 15.5 per cent over the period. The rally, however, has not been uniform. While investors in the leading gainers have enjoyed substantial capital appreciation, several of the stocks carry elevated valuation multiples, while seven companies in the group recorded negative return on equity (ROE), highlighting significant differences in underlying corporate performance. Zichis, SCOA lead gainers on nominal YtD As of August 21, 2026, Zichis Agro Allied Industries topped the ranking with a staggering 365.49 per cent year-to-date (YtD) nominal price gain, narrowly ahead of SCOA Nigeria, which rose 365.19 per cent. They were followed by Union Dicon Salt at 271.09 per cent, RT Briscoe at 241.43 per cent, Infinity Trust Mortgage Bank at 221.43 per cent, Berger Paints Nigeria at 207.50 per cent and Premier Paints at 204 per cent. First Holdco gained 177.08 per cent, while Vitafoam Nigeria advanced 153.04 per cent and Fortis Global Insurance rose 150 per cent. HBM Nigeria appreciated 149.25 per cent. Other major gainers included NGX Group at 123.42 per cent, NCR Nigeria at 121.73 per cent, Julius Berger Nigeria at 103.27 per cent, Aradel Holdings at 102.09 per cent, Morison Industries at 101.94 per cent and Initiates Plc at 100.75 per cent. Completing the group were McNichols at 98.65 per cent, UPDC Real Estate Investment Trust at 97.83 per cent, UACN at 95.44 per cent, May & Baker Nigeria at 94.70 per cent, Zenith Bank at 93.65 per cent and Skyway Aviation Handling Company at 93.56 per cent. Real returns YtD remains strong After adjusting the reported gains for inflation, the analysis indicates that the leading stocks still generated substantial positive real returns. Zichis Agro Allied delivered the highest real gain at 1,379.25 per cent, followed by SCOA Nigeria at 302.8 per cent, Union Dicon Salt at 221.3 per cent and RT Briscoe at 195.61 per cent. Infinity Trust Mortgage Bank recorded 178.3 per cent, while Berger Paints gained 166.2 per cent in real terms. First Holdco returned 139.9 per cent, Vitafoam 119.1 per cent, Fortis Global Insurance 116.5 per cent and HBM Nigeria 115.8 per cent. Other real-return leaders included NGX Group at 93.4 per cent, NCR Nigeria at 91.97 per cent, McNichols at 79 per cent, Julius Berger at 75.9 per cent, Aradel Holdings at 74.9 per cent, Morison Industries at 74.8 per cent, Initiates at 73.8 per cent, UPDC REIT at 71.3 per cent, UACN at 69.2 per cent, May & Baker at 68.6 per cent, Zenith Bank at 67.7 per cent and Skyway Aviation Handling at 67.6 per cent. The figures underline the scale of capital gains available to investors who entered these stocks early. However, high past returns should not be interpreted as a guarantee of future performance, particularly where valuation multiples have expanded faster than earnings. Dividends paying companies Analysis has shown that capital appreciation was not matched by dividend income across the group. Of the stocks for which dividend-yield data were available, HBM Nigeria offered the highest dividend yield at 6.59 per cent, followed by UPDC REIT at 5.35 per cent, Aradel Holdings at 2.40 per cent and NGX Group at 2.26 per cent. Infinity Trust Mortgage Bank yielded 1.56 per cent, May & Baker 1.35 per cent, Julius Berger 1.37 per cent, Vitafoam 1.29 per cent, McNichols 1.24 per cent, Berger Paints 1.12 per cent, Initiates 1.12 per cent, Zichis 0.59 per cent, UACN 0.56 per cent and First Holdco 0.46 per cent. Six companies from the top YtD nominal gainers in price appreciation — SCOA Nigeria, Union Dicon Salt, RT Briscoe, Premier Paints, Fortis Global Insurance and Morison Industries — had no dividend yield because no dividend was declared. Analysts have noted that investors focused on total returns need to distinguish between capital gains and income returns. A stock can produce spectacular price appreciation while offering little or no dividend income. Conversely, a lower-growth stock with a stronger dividend yield may appeal more to income-oriented investors. Some stocks now look expensive The Price-to-Book (P/B) ratios reveal a wide disparity in how the market values the companies relative to their net assets. SCOA Nigeria had the highest reported P/B ratio at 24.85 times, followed by Morison Industries at 12.95 times, NCR Nigeria at 12.05 times, UACN at 7.02 times, Vitafoam at 6.91 times, McNichols at 6.59 times and HBM Nigeria at 6.68 times. Berger Paints traded at 7.90 times book value, Aradel Holdings at 3.96 times, Infinity Trust Mortgage Bank at 3.95 times, Skyway Aviation Handling at 3.60 times, Initiates at 3.08 times and NGX Group at 4.52 times. At the lower end were Zenith Bank at 0.97 times, UPDC REIT at 1.00 times, First Holdco at 1.66 times and Julius Berger at 1.76 times. A high P/B ratio does not automatically mean a company is highly leveraged. Rather, it indicates that investors are paying a substantial premium to the company’s accounting net assets, often because of expectations about future profitability, growth, franchise value or asset quality. Earnings multiples expose valuation risks The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio presents an even sharper divide. Morison Industries recorded an exceptionally high P/E of 3,714.29 times, followed by SCOA Nigeria at 92.99 times, NCR Nigeria at 59.03 times, UACN at 39.54 times and Skyway Aviation Handling at 30.68 times. Berger Paints traded at 24.06 times earnings, Infinity Trust Mortgage Bank at 23.47 times, First Holdco at 20.75 times, NGX Group at 18.50 times, Vitafoam at 16.94 times, Julius Berger at 16.72 times, McNichols at 16.60 times and HBM Nigeria at 15.42 times. May & Baker traded at 11.71 times, Aradel Holdings at 7.82 times, UPDC REIT at 7.35 times, Initiates at 6.11 times and Zenith Bank at just 4.81 times. Exceptionally high P/E ratios can signal that investors have already priced substantial future earnings growth into a stock. If earnings fail to catch up with expectations, the share price can come under pressure even when the underlying company remains profitable. ROE separates strong businesses from speculative rallies The strongest warning signal in the data comes from return on equity. Seven companies reported negative ROE. NCR Nigeria recorded the weakest at -6,540.96 per cent, followed by Fortis Global Insurance at -49.2 per cent and SCOA Nigeria at -40.9 per cent. Morison Industries posted -2.75 per cent, Premier Paints -2.2 per cent, Union Dicon Salt -5.8 per cent, while RT Briscoe also recorded negative ROE. HBM Nigeria recorded the highest positive ROE at 43.3 per cent, followed by Vitafoam at 39.6 per cent, McNichols at 39.8 per cent, May & Baker at 34.1 per cent, Aradel Holdings at 35.2 per cent, NGX Group at 29.1 per cent, Infinity Trust Mortgage Bank at 26 per cent, Initiates at 25 per cent, Zenith Bank at 20.1 per cent, UACN at 17.4 per cent, UPDC REIT at 13.7 per cent, Skyway Aviation Handling at 11.7 per cent, Julius Berger at 10.5 per cent and First Holdco at 7.56 per cent. Analysts/operators’ comment Market analysts and operators opined that some of the price gains did not catch up with fundamentals; hence, they cautioned investors against judging stocks solely by YtD price appreciation. “The headline gains are impressive, but investors need to separate price momentum from fundamental value creation. A stock that has risen several hundred per cent can still offer value if earnings and cash flows are accelerating, but the risk of a valuation correction becomes higher when price appreciation substantially outpaces underlying fundamentals,” the Managing Director of Highcap Securities Limited, David Adonri, said. Another analyst stated that the divergence between valuation and profitability is particularly important. “Some of these stocks have generated extraordinary market returns despite negative or weak returns on shareholders’ equity. That suggests investors should look beyond the price chart and examine earnings quality, debt, cash flow, asset values and the sustainability of the turnaround,” analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited said. On dividend-paying stocks, analyst and Chief Operating Officer at InvestData Consulting, Ambrose Omordion, said: “The market is currently rewarding capital appreciation more strongly than dividend income in several of these counters. For long-term investors, however, sustainable dividends remain an important component of total return, particularly when share-price momentum eventually normalises.” The post How 23 stocks beat inflation appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Prisons Service to establish five industries to empower inmates
items.description: The Ghana Prisons Service (GPS) is planning to establish five prison-based industries to equip inmates with marketable skills and support their reintegration. The initiative will transform existing vocational training programmes into commercially oriented ventures in tailoring, cabinetry, shoemaking, packaging and prefabrication, to enable inmates to gain practical experience and earn income. Mrs Patience Baffoe-Bonnie, Director-General of the GPS, announced this at the 2026 Image of a Woman Conference in Accra on Saturday, held on the theme: “Empowered to Influence, Equipped to Lead, Created to Impact.” She said the Service had realised that traditional skills training, including carpentry and masonry, needed to be redesigned to reflect the interests and economic realities of young people. Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said simply teaching an inmate how to perform a skill was not enough, adding that the Service needed to create an environment in which the skill could become a sustainable source of livelihood. She said the Service was also introducing creative areas such as music, poetry, recital and video production to enable inmates to develop skills suited to their talents and interests. Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said inmates would be encouraged to acquire two or three different vocational skills to improve their prospects for employment or entrepreneurship after release. She said the industrialisation programme formed part of the Service’s broader “Think Prisons 360 Degrees” approach, which sought to address incarceration challenges from prevention through rehabilitation and post-release support. Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said the Service was also exploring mechanics and other production areas and seeking partnerships with businesses and other stakeholders. She said the Service was already producing some goods, including its packaged drinking water, “Campers Mineral water”, and had begun working with Ministries and other partners on initiatives involving the production of items such as tables, chairs and windows using metal and wood. Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said the Service planned to dedicate a period every November to showcase its products, improve their quality, elevate and make them marketable, and demonstrate the productive abilities of inmates. She encouraged businesses with expertise in the identified areas to partner the Service to expand the programme. Mrs Baffoe-Bonniel said the Service was also strengthening post-release support because the transition from prison to freedom could expose former inmates to significant social and economic pressures. She said the Service was engaging schools and churches to educate and encourage young people to make positive life choices. Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said the Service had launched initiatives to mobilise medicines and medical equipment for prison facilities and intended to sustain such support annually. Prophetess Aku Xornam Adzraku-Kevi, Conference Convener and Executive Director of the Purim African Youth Development Platform (PAYDP), said the decision to bring together stakeholders from different sectors was deliberate because women’s empowerment required collaboration beyond one institution or sector. She said PAYDP had worked for years in reproductive health, livelihood empowerment, sexual and gender-based violence, and leadership capacity for women and girls. Prophetess Adzraku-Kevi, also General Overseer of Glorious Abundant Ministries International (GAMI), said the conference provided an opportunity for religious leaders, development partners, civil society organisations, government representatives and other stakeholders to share ideas that could strengthen the organisation’s future programmes. “I believe that we’ve been training women and girls for years, and a lot of the things we are hearing will enhance our mind, our thoughts, and further help us to build the capacity of our women and girls,” she said. Prophetess Adzraku-Kevi encouraged women to rise above barriers and pursue leadership opportunities, saying there was nothing too small for them to achieve. She also called on policymakers to continue improving opportunities for women and noted the growing representation of women in Parliament. The Image of a Woman Conference 2026, organised by PAYDP and GAMI, was inspired by Prophetess Adzraku-Kevi’s book, “The Image of a Woman.” The conference sought to inspire and empower women while creating opportunities for leadership development, mentorship, entrepreneurship, networking and social transformation. It brought together government officials, Members of Parliament, corporate executives, entrepreneurs, development partners, diplomats, faith leaders, students, media personalities and emerging women leaders. The conference also honoured veteran media personality Madam Rosemary Ardayfio for her contribution to journalism, media excellence and mentorship.

items.title: Penalty at the gate: Lagos private schools fine late-pickup parents
items.description: By Elizabeth Adegbesan THE school bell may have signalled the end of classes, but for some parents in Lagos, it is now the beginning of another race — against the clock and, sometimes, against a late-pickup bill. Some private schools in Lagos and a few other major Nigerian cities are increasingly imposing monetary charges on parents who fail to collect their children within stipulated pickup periods. The practice, which is not uniform across schools, is generating a fresh debate among parents, educators and school administrators over where parental responsibility ends and a school’s obligation to care for children after official closing time begins. Some Lagos private schools now have clearly stated late-pickup policies, with charges ranging from fixed fees to amounts calculated according to how long a child remains in school after the designated pickup time. Others offer after-school programmes as an alternative for parents who cannot make it to the school gate before closing time. But for many working parents, particularly those commuting across Lagos, the policy has become a source of anxiety. Traffic congestion, vehicle breakdowns, fuel shortages, unexpected workplace demands and other emergencies can turn what should be a routine school pickup into a prolonged journey. Mr. Jude Okafor, a banker and father of two primary school pupils, said some schools were being insensitive to the realities confronting working parents. “The school management is being completely insensitive to the realities of working in a city,” he lamented. “I leave my office at 3:30 PM, but traffic gridlock can trap you for hours. “Charging me N5,000 because of transit issues is daylight robbery. Schools should support struggling families, not penalise them for structural problems beyond their control.” For Mrs. Gladys Omokheke, a Lagos-based hairstylist, the experience was even more frustrating. She recalled that she once fell asleep and woke up 45 minutes after her daughter’s school closing time. “I saw up to ten missed calls from her class teacher,” she said. “When I got to the school, I was told to pay N2,000 before I could take my child home. “I had to apply force and quarrel to avoid paying such a ridiculous amount. “In our days, teachers found it pleasing to even watch over your children in situations of late pickup. Now, they see every opportunity as a means to make money.” But the anger is not universal. Some parents and educators believe schools have a legitimate reason to discourage habitual late pickup, particularly where parents repeatedly leave children behind long after other pupils have gone home. Mrs. Kafayat Abdul, an educator, supports the policy. “If there is no strict financial penalty, people will continue to abuse the system,” she said. “Some parents live or work just ten minutes away from the campus but routinely leave their kids at school until late evening simply because it is convenient for them. “Teachers are human beings who need to return to their own families. If you want extended care, you should expect to pay for it legally.” ‘ We are not a daycare centre’ School administrators argue that the charges are not necessarily about making money but about dealing with the practical consequences of parents arriving late. Mrs. Jumoke Olanrewaju, a headmistress of a private school, said schools have limited resources and cannot be expected to provide unlimited childcare after official closing time. “We are an educational institution, not a full-time daycare facility,” she said. “When school officially dismisses at 2:00 PM, our teachers’ instructional duties end. Keeping underpaid staff back until 6:00 PM to watch over uncollected children is unsustainable. “It exhausts our personnel and compromises the safety of the pupils in an increasingly volatile security climate where children left late become targets.” The issue is particularly sensitive in Lagos, where the distance between a parent’s workplace and a child’s school can be deceptively short on a map but painfully long during peak traffic. Some schools have therefore opted for a different approach — offering structured after-school care for parents who cannot meet the normal pickup deadline. Readington School in the Lekki area, for instance, advertises late-pickup and after-school facilities, while another Lagos private school provides an after-school service for parents unable to meet its pickup time. Punishment or payment for extra care? This distinction may ultimately determine whether parents see the policy as punitive or reasonable. Where a school provides additional supervision beyond normal hours as a clearly defined service, parents may regard payment as a legitimate childcare cost. But where a parent is unexpectedly delayed by traffic or an emergency and is confronted with a substantial charge, the same payment can feel more like a punishment. The debate is therefore shifting from whether parents should pick up their children on time to a bigger question: should late pickup be treated as misconduct deserving punishment, or as additional childcare requiring payment? The post Penalty at the gate: Lagos private schools fine late-pickup parents appeared first on Vanguard News .
